claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type thin films have bulk-like magnetic-domain structures.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type thin films exhibit an established bulk-like magnetocaloric response.
The unpatterned films exhibit magnetic hysteresis characteristic of bulk-like behavior.
Lithographically confining the films to widths of 10–100 nm reduces magnetic-domain size and coherence.
Narrowing the films into nanoribbons increases their surface-to-volume ratio.
The increased surface-to-volume ratio enhances thermal coupling to the substrate and interfacial heat dissipation.
Large, coherent magnetic domains are necessary for a strong magnetocaloric response in this alloy system.
Reduced lateral dimensions impede the formation of the large, coherent domains needed for a strong magnetocaloric response.
Nanoribbon confinement diminishes the magnetocaloric temperature change relative to the unpatterned film.
Magnetic nanostructure or domain organization can govern hysteresis behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Nanoribbon confinement alters the low-field hysteresis loop relative to the unpatterned film.
The altered hysteresis may appear as reduced loop area or shifted coercivity.
Within the 10–100 nm range, narrower ribbons produce a larger reduction in magnetocaloric temperature change.
Rapid heat dissipation limits the effective magnetic-cooling cycle frequency.
The confinement-induced change in magnetocaloric response is more pronounced at higher cycle frequencies because of heat-transfer limitations.
The proposed mechanism applies to 10–100 nm widths, low applied fields near the magnetic transition, and approximately 0.1–10 Hz cycling.

contradictions.description: Enhanced thermal coupling and more rapid heat dissipation are said to limit the effective cycle frequency and to cause stronger heat-transfer limitations at higher frequency. Faster thermal coupling would ordinarily alleviate a heat-transfer-rate bottleneck; the hypothesis does not explain the competing time constants needed to reconcile these causal directions.
